method.filter: median over 9 samples (0.9 s); samples outside 49–51 Hz are gaps and read as 50 Hz
method.event: fall of more than 100 mHz within 5 s, at least 2 min after the previous one; nadir is the minimum within 20 s
method.event_time: `t` is the start of the 5 s window the fall is detected in, so the fall itself begins up to 5 s later; the featured trace's `event_index` is `t`
method.on_hour: a fall within 20 s of the hour is a market-schedule step, not a trip, and is excluded from trip counts
method.why_filter: the raw series has 1–2-sample spikes (one reads 48.86 Hz between two 50.07 Hz samples); a raw minimum would report near-misses that never happened

events.caveat: A fixed threshold counts more events when inertia is low, because the same loss falls further; the spring–summer cluster cannot be split between low inertia and more trips until each event is paired with its hour's kinetic energy.

figures.text: After the reference incident the instantaneous frequency minimum shall stay at or above 49.0 Hz; indiscriminate load shedding starts at 48.8 Hz.
The reference incident is the loss of Oskarshamn 3 at 1,450 MW. Olkiluoto 3 counts as 1,300 MW because its protection scheme sheds 300 MW of load when it trips.
FCR-D alone keeps the frequency above 49.0 Hz after the reference incident down to 150 GWs.
120 GWs is the stability design level; stability is challenged around 90 GWs.
At 100 GWs, roughly 300 MW of FFR in the Nordic system keeps the frequency minimum above 49.0 Hz after the reference incident. Procurement adds a margin for model and forecast error.
The extra kinetic energy needed to raise the frequency minimum by 0.1 Hz in an 80 GWs system is 20 GWs.
Nordic kinetic energy, pre-disturbance, per year.
FFR activates fully within 1.3 s at 49.7 Hz, 1.0 s at 49.6 Hz or 0.7 s at 49.5 Hz. Fingrid procures 0–60 MW, only in low-inertia hours, mostly spring to autumn.

limitations: Which unit tripped is not in the open data; events are unattributed.
Frequency is measured at Finnish 400 kV substations; the Nordic system shares one frequency, but local oscillation is not separated.
Kinetic energy is itself an operator estimate.
Finland's FFR is one share of a Nordic need.
Our model is one-bus and fitted to published design points; it draws shapes and is never quoted as a figure.
No event in the window came near 49.0 Hz; the story is about margin, not a near-miss.
